provenance: Derived TWICE, independently, by two agents that saw no implementation (none existed) and did not see each other. Committed BEFORE any verdict code was written, per REQ-04 as strengthened by the kickoff attack panel: expected values taken from the code under test prove only that the code agrees with itself.
form_note: centre = (2np + z^2) / (2(n + z^2)); halfw = z*sqrt(z^2 + 4np(1-p)) / (2(n + z^2)). z^2 is z*z, never a literal. The half-width uses 4*n*p*(1-p), NOT 4*x*(n-x)/n. p-l and u-p are literal subtractions, never replaced by halfw. l and u are clamped into [0,1] AFTER the roots are computed. Every one of those rules changes the last bits if broken - see ADR-0311.
disagreement: The two independent derivations agreed bit-for-bit on only 2 of 8 cases (B and G). Elsewhere they differed by 1-24 ULP because one used the algebraically identical p-form. Checked against 60-digit exact arithmetic, NEITHER form is correctly rounded; both sit 5-20 ULP from the true value. Bit-for-bit across independent implementations is therefore not achievable, which is what ADR-0311 records and what the `strict` flag below marks.

assertions.bit_for_bit: every case must reproduce `lower` and `upper` exactly, against the pinned tree
assertions.strict_cases: cases with strict:true were reproduced bit-for-bit by BOTH independent derivations, so they are the only values known to be reproducible by an implementation sharing no code with this one

invariants.bounds: 0 <= l <= p <= u <= 1 for every arm, AFTER clamping
invariants.containment: lower <= d <= upper for every case
invariants.upper_not_clamped: UPPER may exceed 1 (cases E and G). Newcombe's method does not guarantee containment in [-1,1]; truncating it would change the method.

cases.note: the realistic case: a ~2pp lift at n~1900 per arm
zero successes in BOTH arms. The pinned form returns l=0 exactly; the p-form returns a NEGATIVE probability (-2.16e-19), which is why the form is pinned.

all successes in BOTH arms. NOT the mirror of C: |lower| differs from C by 228 ULP, a pure floating-point asymmetry between computing near 0 and near 1. An implementation asserting LOWER(n,0,n,0) == -LOWER(n,n,n,n) will fail.
small n, huge effect. UPPER exceeds 1 and is NOT clamped.
identical proportions: d is exactly +0 (not -0) and LOWER must be negative

n=1 knife-edge. In EXACT arithmetic LOWER == d == 1; in doubles it lands one ULP below. Any promote rule keyed on LOWER against a threshold near the point estimate is decided by a rounding bit. Both derivations agreed bit-for-bit.
a tiny effect at large n - the case a floor is supposed to refuse. LOWER is negative, so no verdict.
